books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.text:
“...all freedmen, free negroes and mulattoes in this State, over the age of eighteen years, found on the second Monday in January, 1866, or thereafter, with no lawful employment or business, or found unlawfully assembling themselves together, either in the day or night time, and all white persons so assembling themselves with freedmen, free negroes or mulattoes, or usually associating with freedmen, free negroes or mulattoes, on terms of equality, or living in adultery or fornication with a freed woman, free negro or mulatto, shall be deemed vagrants. . . .”

—Mississippi Vagrant Law, part of the Mississippi Black Code, 1865
stimulus.source_note: Mississippi Vagrant Law (1865), Laws of Mississippi, 1865. Public domain. Wording verified against the transcription of the Laws of Mississippi text. Leading and trailing ellipses mark omitted text.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The law quoted here was mainly meant to

options.text: give freedpeople land of their own.
options.misconception: Background: the law says nothing about land, and Mississippi barred freedpeople from renting farmland outside towns.
Background: the law threatened freedpeople with fines and jail, so it endangered them rather than protecting them.

options.text: force freedpeople back into plantation labor.
let freedpeople vote in state elections.
options.misconception: Background: the law is about labor and movement, and Black men did not yet have the vote.

rationales.A: Background: the law says nothing about land, and Mississippi barred freedpeople from renting farmland outside towns.
rationales.B: Background: the law threatened freedpeople with fines and jail, so it endangered them rather than protecting them.
rationales.C: Anyone without a job or a written contract was called a vagrant, fined, and hired out to an employer. With land closed off and movement policed, the only open door led back to the plantation.
rationales.D: Background: the law is about labor and movement, and Black men did not yet have the vote.
rationales.general:
1. The law calls a freedperson with no job a vagrant, and fines and jails vagrants.
2. Background: freedpeople owned almost no land and could not rent farmland outside towns.
3. So the choice the law left was signing a labor contract or being hired out by the sheriff.
4. That is slavery’s labor system rebuilt with fines instead of chains.
Remember: a law that punishes joblessness is often a law that forces people into a job.
